Massif is a map editor for Minecraft Java worlds in the spirit of WorldPainter, with a node-based terrain generator in the spirit of Gaea, written in Rust.

## New in 1.2.3

**Render side: Blender's denoiser, smooth edges, quiet woods**

With Intel's Open Image Denoise (the denoiser of Blender's Cycles), the Render side denoises with it as the samples settle and denoises the images it saves: one sample through it is already nearer the finished image than four raw ones. The image is anti-aliased as Cycles filters its pixels, the textures are averaged where they are smaller than a pixel, and far leaves and glass add up to how solid they are, so that woods seen from afar settle smooth instead of flickering in a pattern of pixels.

**Open Image Denoise comes with Massif**

Massif's builds for macOS, Windows and Linux now carry Intel's Open Image Denoise 2.5.1, the denoiser Blender's Cycles uses, so the Render side denoises with it everywhere; its licence (Apache-2.0) and third-party notices are in the app's folder. Where it cannot load, the Render side keeps its own denoiser on the graphics card.

**A calmer Render side: denoised while moving, lighter, looks that hold**

While the view moves, the Render side draws at half the resolution and denoises every frame, so it never shows raw grain; on a Retina screen it draws a pixel a point, as Blender does by default, a quarter of the work, and it sends the graphics card one sample at a time and none while Massif is in the background, so the rest of the app no longer lags. A sky Look now sets everything it owns, the Night and the Blue hour exposed so they can be seen, and moves the camera path's keyframes to its hour instead of being undone by them; touching a setting afterwards shows Custom. Fog is set by how far one sees through it (40 to 4000 blocks), so it can no longer wash the whole image out white, and the Timeline's frames a second stay between 12 and 60.

**The Render side denoises, and shows edits made elsewhere**

The Render side's image no longer starts as black grain: Denoise, on at first in Render Output, smooths the noise of the first samples away while they add up, the textures and the edges of the blocks kept sharp, and fades as the image settles (one sample denoised is about as clean as four raw ones, seven as sixteen). Saving an image can denoise it too. A new Clamp indirect setting cuts down the rare bright specks of a bounce, so that the image settles sooner, and a sample gone wrong no longer leaves a black pixel until the view moves. Coming back to the Render side after the map was edited, or after it had to build its scene anew, the view shows the new image: it could stay frozen on the old one, whatever the camera did. A map grown on the World side is built again whole.

**Color Management as in Blender**

Render Output has Blender's Color Management: the View Transform (Standard, Khronos PBR Neutral, AgX by default, Filmic, Filmic Log, False Color, Raw), its Look (AgX's None, Punchy, Greyscale and contrasts from Very High to Very Low; Filmic's contrasts), the Exposure in stops and the Gamma. AgX and Filmic keep shadows soft and let bright colours whiten instead of burning to a hue; the stills, the videos and the denoised view all go through the same transform.

**Render the Timeline as a video**

Render Output has an Animation to save section: Render animation… draws the Timeline's camera path frame by frame, each frame denoised like a still, and saves it as an MP4 video (on macOS, through the system's own encoder) or as numbered PNG images, with the frames done, the time left and Cancel; PNG images asked again into the same folder go on from where they stopped. The Timeline also answers Blender's keys: Space plays, I or K keeps a keyframe, Alt+I removes it, the arrows step a frame or jump between keyframes, Shift with them goes to the start or the end, and Home frames the whole map.

**Walk through the Render view**

The Render Viewport walks as Blender's walk navigation does: hold the right button to look around from where the camera stands, W A S D to move where you look, Q and E to go down and up, Shift to go faster, and the wheel, while walking, to set the speed. The image stays denoised at reduced resolution while you move. Sliding the view moved to the middle button.

**The Render view moves as Blender's**

Dragging turns about the point under the pointer, Shift-drag slides it with the pointer, and the wheel comes closer to the point under the pointer, every speed by the distance to what is there, so that two blocks over the grass and two kilometres over the map are both easy to reach; double-click comes in close on a point, the numeric pad gives the front, side and top views, and W A S D go by their places on the keyboard. The Camera panel gives the eye's location in numbers, and Lock Camera to View with Align Camera to View keep the camera of stills, keyframes and the video apart from the view, as in Blender.

**Keyed settings and Blender's sections on the Render side**

The sun, the sky, the haze, the fog, the clouds, the hour, the exposure and the lens can be keyed over the Timeline as in Blender: click the diamond beside a setting, or press I over it, to keep its value at the playhead, Alt+I to take the key away; settings ease from key to key and the video draws them. The Render panels are arranged in Blender's sections (Sampling, Light Paths, Color Management, Grass, Output), each folded by a click on its title, with a Viewport samples setting where the view stops.

**Mist in the valleys**

The Render side's fog and mist now lie on the floor of the map's own valleys, measured from the scene, instead of a fixed height over the sea, so they look right on any map; Foggy morning is a thinner layer with clear air above, and a new Valley mist look lays a bright mist in the low ground at sunrise.

**Blades of grass on the Render side**

Render Output has a Grass setting: the game's Blocks, or Blades, a field of thin blades of grass over every grass block in the place of the short and tall grass and the ferns, each its own height and lean, in tufts, darker at the foot and lighter and yellower toward the tip, in the grass's own colours, shading each other and taking the sun's shadows, the flowers left as they are. Density and Height set how many blades a block and how tall. Far off the field thins out to the grass blocks under it. Blades take some twice as long to draw at the grass's height.

**More realistic blades of grass**

The Render side's Blades of grass look like a meadow: thinner and many more of them, each bent along a curve to a fine tip and rounded, darker and cooler at the foot and lighter and yellower toward the tip, a few dry ones among them, combed as by the wind and taller in patches, the sun shining through them from behind and the ground between them in the grass's shade rather than its pixels. Tall grass and large ferns become taller blades. The Grass setting now comes first in Render Output.

**A minimap in the Render view**

A map button at the top right of the Render view shows the whole map small in a corner, with the camera and what it sees and the Timeline's camera path, so you always know where you are; click on it to put the camera over that place, its height and direction kept, or drag to slide it. The choice is remembered.

**OpenEXR height maps and renders**

Massif reads and writes OpenEXR, the float image format of Gaea, World Machine, Houdini and Blender. A height map in EXR (half or 32-bit floats, its `Y` channel or the brightness of its colours) can make a new map, be painted with Edit ▸ Import mask… or feed the Terrain Generator's Heightmap and Image nodes, at full precision: the file's lowest and highest values are shown and black and white start at those heights, so heights in blocks come back where they were. File ▸ Export Height Map… and the Generator Viewer's Height map: Save… offer OpenEXR beside the 16-bit PNG, with each column's height in blocks. On the Render side, Save image… can write an OpenEXR of the light as traced, linear and before the view transform, brighter than white where the sun is, with depth, normals and albedo as layers of the same file for compositing.

**Shaders in the 3D View**

A Shaders button (the sun) in the 3D View's header gives the view the look of a Minecraft shader pack, without loading one: the sun casts shadows, the hills' over the whole map and the trees' and buildings' on the ground around them, blocks are shaded where others close in on them, the sunlight is warmer and the shade a little bluer, and the colours go through the Render side's AgX. It is off at first and stays as you leave it.

**Several Dioramas at once**

The Diorama can be open in several areas at once, as the 3D View can: each has its own place, zoom, turn and Surface or Caves, and the layout keeps what each shows, so you can watch the surface and the caves side by side.

**Apply to map twice as fast, and the Diorama follows it**

The Terrain Generator's Apply to map takes about half the time it did: a volcanic archipelago written over a map of 8192 × 8192 blocks went from 17.7 s to 7.5 s, of 4096 × 4096 from 6.4 s to 4.0 s, with the very same map as a result. The Archipelago node no longer works out the coast of islands too far away to matter, the Volcano node its relief away from the volcanoes, and the blocks the graph's colours pick are found in parallel. The Diorama, open while a graph is applied that makes the map another size, showed the old map's squares, some of them with the new map in them: it now draws the new map whole.

**Measure the map, and a tidier Info panel**

A Measure tool, in the Navigate row of the Tools panel, measures the map as a block is a metre. Drag a line, or click a path of points, and it tells the distance on the map and along the ground, the heights at its ends, the mean and steepest slopes in percent and degrees, with the profile of the land under it; point at the profile and the map marks the spot. Switch to Area and drag or click around a part of the map: its area in m² or km², its perimeter, its lowest, highest and mean heights, the blocks over and under its lowest ground, the sea level or a height you choose (what levelling it would take), the share under water, and the share of each terrain, biome and layer that covers it. It works in the 3D views too, Esc or a right-click clears it, and Keep on screen leaves it shown with the other tools; measures are never saved in the map. The Info panel is laid out anew in Position (now with the chunk and region file), Ground, Layers here and Measure, which shows the results of the measure.

**Travel times and the Travel range tool**

The Measure tool's label now says what its numbers are, "21.06 km · ↓54 blocks · slope 10 %", and tells how long the line takes to travel in Minecraft: point at the label, or look in the Info panel, for the time walking, sprinting, sprint-jumping, on a fast horse, by boat on water or ice, by minecart and with an elytra and rockets, in Minecraft days too once past one (a day is 20 minutes). A new Travel range tool, in the Navigate row, draws rings around the pointer on the map and on the land in the 3D views: how far players get in a time, each ring a time in minutes or Minecraft days and a way of going, set in Tool Settings (one and two days on foot at first). The rings are straight and flat, the farthest one gets; a click pins them, Esc lets them go.

**A Spawn point tool, as WorldPainter's**

The spawn point is now a point on the map rather than numbers in File ▸ World Information alone. The new **Spawn point** tool, in the Navigate group of the Tools panel, puts it on the ground where you click, on the 2D map or in a 3D view, as one step to undo; a pin marks it on the map and in the 3D views, and dragging the pin on the map moves it. With Pan or the Spawn point tool in hand, a right-click on the map offers **Set spawn here**. World Information still shows and sets its numbers.

**Auto paint styles, and Auto biome keeps deserts**

Auto paint has a Style at the top of its Tool Settings: Follow biome, as before, or Temperate forest, Jungle, Mountain, Desert, Badlands, Taiga, Snowy, Savanna, Coast and Swamp, which paint the land by its shape (shore, ground, hills, mountains, peaks, cliffs, under water) whatever its biomes, so that a desert can be painted as a jungle. Custom sets each part's terrain, Save as preset keeps it under a name of yours, Delete takes it out. Auto biome no longer turns a desert into plains: a column keeps the biome it has when its ground agrees with it (a desert on sand, as the Terrain Generator's climate paints it, badlands on red sand, a savanna, taiga or jungle on grass, snowy biomes on snow), and a map mostly of sand is a desert rather than plains. Its Tool Settings list what the preview's colours stand for: each biome the rules give, with the kinds of land that get it, and the hatching.

**Sort terrains by dragging, and choose their map colour**

In the Terrain panel, drag a terrain onto another to put it before or after it, as the Layers panel's layers: an accent line shows where it goes, it can land in another category that way, and each move is one step to undo. Right-click a terrain ▸ Map colour to choose the colour it is drawn in on the 2D map and in its swatches; Auto gives it back its own colour, from its blocks. Both are saved with the map, and neither changes the export.

**Massif says why part of a stroke shows no change**

When a brush stroke leaves part of the map looking as it was, a word at the foot of the window says how much of the stroke, and why: a ground cover of blocks lies over the terrain painted (as a WorldPainter map's custom ground covers of sand or gravel do, the terrain being painted under them), a level stands over the one painted, a layer is locked, the brush's filter leaves those columns, or the layer painted is hidden on the map. The Info panel says the same of the column under the cursor for the tool in hand.

**Smoothing a coast no longer raises the water**

Smoothing, lowering or flattening the land by the sea could leave patches of water above the sea level (at 65 by a sea at 63, with straight, blocky edges), most of all on maps from WorldPainter. Land lowered under the sea's level now holds the sea's water, never higher, and the water beside it fills it as before; lakes made with Flood keep their own level.

**The Generator Graph takes Blender's keys, and the Volcano loses its line.** Over the graph, the node editor's keys of Blender work as there, Ctrl as ⌘ on a Mac: Shift A adds a node at the pointer, Tab opens the composite selected and leaves it, ⌘A, Alt A and ⌘I select all, none or the others, B draws a box from the next press, L and Shift L add what feeds the selection or what it feeds, G moves the selection with the pointer and Shift D duplicates and moves (a click puts down, Esc puts back), ⌘X removes the selected nodes and wires what they fed from what fed them, M bypasses (it was B), H folds, ⌘G and ⌘⇧G (or ⌘⌥G) make and undo a composite, ⌘J frames, F shows the whole graph and the numpad's dot the selected nodes. The nodes' menus name their keys, and the help lists them all. The Volcano node no longer draws a straight line west of each volcano, where its gullies did not meet as they went round; its gullies fall in other places than before.

**A clearer Generator Viewer bar.** What you see and what is done to the map are apart now. The sliders beside 2D/3D and Clay/Colours open the View options, which never touch the map: relief, contour lines, mask opacity, sun height, background, and the resolution, now buttons from Auto to 8K, so that choosing one no longer closes the options. On the right, after a line, Live, Apply to map, and the arrow beside it with Keep the map's ground (formerly Apply over the map) and Height map Save…, each saying what it does to the map. Whether node thumbnails are in clay or in colours is a setting of the graph now, Node thumbnails, in Node Properties with no node selected.

**Mixed covers stay one terrain, mixes show mixed in 3D, steep slopes smoothed**

Making a WorldPainter map's covers of layers the ground's own (on import, or Edit ▸ Covers of Layers to Ground…) no longer splits a cover of several blocks into a terrain a block ("Mixed Upland Layer", "Mixed Upland Layer 2"… each of one block): it makes one terrain of the cover's blocks, mixed in its weights, over the terrain it lies on, and one more named "… on …" for each other terrain it covers; where the terrain's top already has all the cover's blocks it stays as it is. The 3D View draws the smoothed layers and slabs of a terrain of several blocks in the block each column has, as the export writes them: a mix such as WorldPainter's custom terrains no longer looks all of its first block with the others only along the steps. Smooth terrain fills the foot of steep slopes too, where the land beside is two blocks or more higher, with half a block of layers or a stair as at a step of one block (vertical slabs, where allowed, still stand against cliffs); gentle slopes are as before.

**Names of your exports**

Settings ▸ Export has a File names template for everything you export: worlds, schematics, height maps, render images and animations, and Share Image pictures. Build it from `{name}`, `{kind}`, `{date}`, `{time}`, `{timestamp}`, `{counter}`, `{size}` and `{version}`, or pick a ready one; the date can be ISO (2026-11-27), European or US and the time 24 h or 12 h, and a preview shows the name it makes. Characters Windows or macOS refuse are replaced, and the save dialog opens in the folder of your last export with a name that is free there, adding -2, -3 rather than offering to overwrite a file.

**Compact mode**

Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Compact mode puts the top of the window on a single row, for small screens: New, Open, Save and Export, then the sides and the workspaces, then the map's title as a menu (World Information, Save Point, Versions, Save As) and Versions on the right. The favourite tools stay in the Tools panel and Undo and Redo in the Edit menu, the workspaces scroll sideways in a narrow window, and the panels sit closer together. In both modes the top bars lose the lines that doubled the edge under them.

**Show in Explorer opens the right folder on Windows**

After an export or a save, the message's button now opens the world's folder in Explorer with the world selected, where it left Explorer at This PC when the path came with forward slashes (as launchers such as CurseForge or Prism write them) or with Windows' long-path prefix. A path deleted since shows the nearest folder still there. The button says Show in Explorer on Windows and Show in folder on Linux, and Massif's brushes folder opens the same way.

## New in 1.2.2

**Erosion, rebuilt: real valleys in a fraction of a second**

The Terrain Generator's **Erosion** is new (Stream erosion's second version): rivers cut valleys that branch up every slope with sharp ridges between them, the slopes creep and slide, and what the water carries fills the valley floors and spreads into fans, worked out coarse to fine over the whole terrain so that Apply window by window leaves no seams. Its settings are Gaea's: Duration, Downcutting, Erosion scale, Sediment removal, Rock softness and Base level, with Flow, Wear, Deposition and Sediment masks for colours and layers. It is about a hundred times quicker than Stream erosion (0.66 s instead of 83 s for a simulation of 2048²), and on the relief bench its valleys come twice as close to Monte Perdido's and the Grand Canyon's. The Alpine Range composite uses it. Graphs made before keep Stream erosion and their results; in MassifScript a call now makes the latest version of a node, an older one being written `Erosion@1(…)` or `Transform@1(…)`.

**One terrain generator: the classic graph is converted**

The Terrain Generator is now Massif's only generator: the classic graph, with its Classic graph, Graph Viewport, Classic properties and Render Settings panels and its Graph and Render workspaces, is gone. A map made with it opens with its graph converted into the Terrain Generator's, node by node, with the same settings, links and places: what ran 1.2's own code (the classic Erosion, rivers, lakes, the sea, floating islands, overhangs, tectonic plates, Auto colour) and plain arithmetic (Constant, Levels, Clamp, Combine…) make the same terrain, and the nodes built on noise keep their shape and settings with the Terrain Generator's noises, so their relief is close rather than the same. A map that has a Terrain Generator graph of its own keeps it to drive the map, the converted nodes waiting below it, unwired, in a frame titled From the classic graph; a notice says once how many nodes were converted and which are close. A new map made from a template, and the samples of the home screen, get their template as a Terrain Generator graph, applied at once. Saved layouts that showed the classic panels open with the generator's in their place.

**The Generator Viewer takes over from the Graph Viewport**

The Generator Viewer opens in 3D under the sky, as the classic graph's viewport did, and shows a graph's whole result there: the water of its rivers and lakes and its layers of rock over the ground, such as floating islands and overhangs. A map made from a template, or a sample, is seen as its template is best seen, with its own sun, clouds, haze and sea. The viewer is taller in the Generator workspace. Its settings menu gains Apply over the map, where what the graph digs and raises goes into levels of their own and the map's ground stays as it was, and Height map: Save…, which saves the terrain as a 16-bit PNG height map without writing it into the map.

**Mountain, Transform and a Combine with as many inputs as you connect**

The Terrain Generator gains light pieces to build a landscape from, as in Gaea. **Mountain** makes one mountain from six settings (Scale, Height, Style, Bulk, Reduce details, Seed), at about half the cost of Alpine mountains. **Transform** now moves, turns, scales, stretches and deforms a relief at full detail instead of at the simulations' resolution (graphs made with the earlier Transform keep it and their results). **Combine** takes any number of reliefs: an empty input appears as soon as the last one is connected, each with a mask of its own, combined by one of eleven modes; in MassifScript it is `Mixer(a, b, c, mode: "max")`. A relief bench, `tools/relief_bench.sh`, measures the generator's shapes against real mountains, canyons, hills and a volcano.

**Grow your own trees.** Objects ▸ **Grow trees…** grows trees from a few settings instead of schematic files: start from an oak, spruce, birch, cherry, palm, willow, acacia, dead tree or one of two giants (a giant sequoia about a hundred blocks tall, a great oak), then change its height, trunk, limbs, how much they droop or reach for the sun, the shape of the crown, the leaves and the blocks. Trunks flare into roots smoothed with stairs and slabs, branches thin from logs to walls to fences into crowns with gaps, and leaves gather where the twigs end and never decay; **Survival friendly** keeps to logs and leaves. A picture shows the tree and the next seeds' beside it, and a click adds as many variants as you like to a new object layer or to the one picked, with their bushes and small trees for Tree sizes. Trees taller than the room left under the top of the world are no longer cut off there: they are left out.

**A part of the map as a schematic.** File ▸ Export Selection as Schematic… (or Export as Schematic… under the selection in a selection tool's settings) writes the selected columns as a WorldEdit `.schem` (Sponge version 3, or version 2 for WorldEdit 7.2) or a Litematica `.litematic`, with the blocks the export to Minecraft writes there: the ground, the water, the caves, the plants, the trees and the structures with their chests and signs, from a depth under the lowest ground (or the world's floor) to the highest block, biomes included. Before anything is saved, the dialog shows the box's size, the file's size, the materials it holds, the most first with their icons, and the trees of each object layer, and copies them as text. In an object layer's list, Export as .schem… writes the objects picked, a file each, and Grow trees… its trees.

**Share a picture of your map in one click.** File ▸ Share Image… draws pictures of the open map ready to post on Discord or Reddit, and shows them as a carousel: the map as a diorama block, a low-sun view of its most dramatic relief, the map from above with a scale and a north arrow, and the map beside its relief. A slim band gives the map's name, its size and the version of Minecraft, with Massif's mark; it can be light, dark or left out. Pick 16:9, square or 4K, then Copy the picture to paste it anywhere, or Save it as a PNG.

**WorldPainter worlds import with their mods and their layers made ground**

Importing a WorldPainter world first asks for the mods it uses (the game's version, the mods' jars or a modpack's instance, remembered for next time), whether to make its covers of layers the ground's own, and whether to smooth the terrain. With both on, as they are at first, a Conquest Reforged map opens with its grass layers and Forest Floors already part of the land at its own height, the whole map smoothed with layers and no seam where a cover ended, with nothing left to do in the import report. Edit ▸ Covers of Layers to Ground… still does it later.

**Covers of layers made ground leave no seam**

Making a WorldPainter map's covers of layers the ground's own (Conquest Reforged's grass layers, a Forest Floor) no longer raises the covered ground a block over the ground beside it. The layers take the place of the top of the land at its own precise height, and the whole map is smoothed with layers, the ground that had no cover too, so the two meet level as one layered terrain, with no step where a cover ended.

**Layers are sorted by dragging.** In the Layers panel, drag a layer onto another of its kind to put it above or below it, a line in the accent showing where it will go: in a palette, to put the layers a WorldPainter import brought in scattered back in order, or in a section. Dropped on a layer of another palette, it joins that palette at that place. Each move is one step to undo and is saved with the map; the order only changes the list, never the export. Move up and Move down in a layer's menu are steps to undo too.

**Annotation layers in palettes follow their palette.** An annotation layer sorted into a palette is listed there only, no longer among the Annotations' colours too, and the palette's eye shows or hides it even while all the annotations are hidden: a Placeholders palette shown draws its layers. The eye of all the annotations shows or hides the colours and the layers in no palette. As in WorldPainter, the layer you start painting with (a ground cover, trees, an annotation colour or layer) is made visible, whichever eye hid it. An annotation layer can now be removed from its menu, its marks with it, as one step to undo.

**Lua scripts make terrains, ground covers and object layers, and a busy graphics card no longer closes Massif.** A Lua script can now make the map's own terrains from strata of blocks (`map:add_terrain`), ground covers of the plants it names (`map:add_cover`) and object layers of the schematics in its folder (`map:add_objects`, which also retunes an existing layer, a tree pack's included, without its files), each redefined when its name is given again, and read or move the spawn with `map.spawn`; all of it is one step to undo, as anything else a script changes. When the graphics card is busy with another program and does not give the window its image in time, Massif skips that frame and sets the window up again on the next one, instead of closing; it writes this in its log.

**The 3D View keeps its colours when the graphics preset changes**

Picking another preset in Settings ▸ Graphics while a 3D View was open turned its land black, only the water and the outlines still drawn, until the map was opened again. The view now sends the blocks' colours and textures to the graphics card again whenever the preset makes it start its drawing anew.

**The map's crosshair marks the middle of the view.** The crosshair chosen in Settings ▸ Appearance is now drawn at the middle of the 2D map's view, as at the middle of the player's view, to show where the view is centred, instead of under the brush. The pointer keeps the system's crosshair with a white dot, which reads on dark land as on snow.

**Palette blocks can be removed, and a Noise preset is named at once**

In a block palette of your own (Edit palettes…, as when importing a world), the ✕ beside a block of a layer removes it again, as does Remove in its right-click menu; before, the click picked the layer instead, and the same went for the layer's own ✕ and its fields. Saving a Noise pattern as a preset now puts the cursor in its name field as soon as the menu opens, so you can type the name straight away; Enter saves it and Escape leaves without saving.

**Pictures in the manual, and a box gone from the Terrain Generator**

The manual now shows the app in 58 pictures where it named them, from the workspaces and tools to the Terrain Generator. In the Terrain Generator, a setting driven by a mask is listed among the node's inputs under its own name with its diamond socket, instead of a sign that showed as an empty box.

## New in 1.2.1

**The Generator Viewer's 3D looks like the Graph Viewport**

In 3D, the Terrain Generator's viewer now draws the generator's output with the same renderer as the classic Graph Viewport: a sky with soft light, clouds, the sea at the world's sea level, the sides of the terrain, and a camera you turn, move and zoom freely. Its bar at the foot opens the render settings (sun, clouds, haze, exposure), turns clouds and the sea on, frames the relief and saves the view as an image. Clay or colours, the dark background or the sky, the relief and the resolution keep working as before, and Shift + drag still turns the sun.

**A shorter Terrain panel list.** The panel chooser's Terrain section now lists the Terrain Generator's four panels alone: Generator Graph, Generator Viewer, Node Library and Node Properties. The classic graph's panels (Classic graph, Graph Viewport, Classic properties, Render Settings) move to a Classic generator section of their own, offered only for a map made with the classic graph or while one of them is open.

**Annotation layers paint in their own colour, and placeholders import as annotations.** The Annotations brush painted every colour of the map's own (the annotation layers, as WorldPainter's custom ones, imported or made in Massif) in black, the last of WorldPainter's fifteen colours; it now paints each in its own colour, as curves already did. And a WorldPainter layer set not to be exported, a placeholder marking where something goes, now imports as an annotation layer of its name, marked where it was painted, rather than as the plants or blocks it holds.

**Villages: walls round their houses, and a selected village no longer slows the app**

A village's walls (fences, hedges, palisade, ramparts…) now run round the buildings it actually has, a few blocks out from them with rounded corners and a gate wherever a road leaves, instead of a ring round its area that left houses outside and crossed empty land; they follow the village when it is moved, resized, of another theme or density, or when one of its buildings is moved with the Building tool. A village selected with the Structures tool no longer brings the app down to a few frames a second: the line saying how its land suits it was read again from the whole map on every frame, and is now read once each time the map changes.

**Smooth ground covers of WorldPainter follow slopes**

A custom ground cover set Smooth in WorldPainter (Conquest Reforged's grass layers, a Forest Floor mixing layers and small stones) used to come out of the export as whole blocks, a full step at every block on a slope, wherever it was not made the ground's own. It is now laid as WorldPainter lays it: as thick as it is over the ground's precise height, each block of layers in the mix ending in that height's eighths and the other blocks whole, the ground under it left whole, whether the cover lies alone or under other covers. Maps imported before keep their covers whole: import the world again to get it.

**A guide rewritten area by area.** The guide now has a page for each part of Massif, in the order you meet them: getting started (install, a first map, the samples), the window and its panel chooser, the map view, every tool, painting, layers, annotations and annotation layers, water, levels, caves, structures and villages with the Building tool, the 3D views, True Colour, mods and resource packs, importing, every option of the export dialog, working together, scripting and the command line. The Terrain graphs guide opens on the Terrain Generator's four panels, composites, the Map Output, Live and Apply and MassifScript, the classic graph of older maps after it, and the Lua scripting guide gains worked examples. The in-app help names the panels and workspaces as they are in 1.2.1.

**Resource packs over mods' blocks.** A resource pack now goes over every mod's own look in True Colour, the Blocks panel and the 3D views, as in the game, whatever the order its chip and the mods' were added in: a pack that retextures or recolours a mod's blocks (ArdaCraft's pack over Conquest Reforged's grasses and leaves) shows its textures, models and OptiFine colour maps rather than the mod's. Packs still read in their chips' order among themselves, the last one winning, which makes it easy to try a pack across a whole map.

**Annotation layers overlap, and sort into palettes, as in WorldPainter.** WorldPainter's fifteen annotation colours still take each other's place on a block, but each annotation layer (a named colour of the map's own, as WorldPainter's custom annotation layers) is now a layer of its own: several mark the same blocks, over the colours and over each other, so they work as masks for biomes, tree sizes, flow lines or the land's colours. The brush and curves paint the one picked over what is there and the right button rubs out that one alone; the map and the 3D view draw each in its colour and opacity, the Info panel lists every one on the block, and a filter's Only on finds each wherever it is. A WorldPainter map brings its custom annotation layers and its layers set not to be exported in this way, overlaps kept, each in the palette it was sorted into ("Colours", "Placeholders"), and the Layers panel shows them in their palettes with the other layers: the palette's eye and solo show and hide them too, and their menu moves them to another palette, finds them or shows them alone.

**Solo in the Terrain panel works as WorldPainter's.** The Terrain panel's **Solo** now shows only the ground: every ground cover, object and annotation layer is hidden on the map and in 3D, and they come back as they were when it ends. What Solo did before, fading every terrain but the one in hand to see where it is painted, is now **Isolate this terrain**, beside it.

**No more lines of land across the water of a real place**

The relief of a real place no longer draws thin straight lines of land or shallow water across its sea and lakes, nor rows of dots on the open water. The elevation tiles give the water's surface in rectangles of their sources, each flat at a slightly different height, and where two of them met, the strip read between them came out a hair above the water. That strip is now water at the level of the water beside it, so the sea stays sea all the way across.

**WorldPainter custom terrains keep their mix, and Only on asks for everything listed**

A WorldPainter custom terrain imports as one terrain that lays its blocks as WorldPainter does: a noise mix block by block, a blob mix in patches of about the blobs' size, and a layered mix by height in the world (repeating and sloping as it was set), where it used to become a plain mix of its blocks whatever its mode, so a terrain of layers showed every block everywhere. A brush's **Only on** now works as WorldPainter's: with a layer and a terrain listed (meadow fescue and dirt), it paints only where that layer lies on that terrain, rather than wherever either is; two terrains, two biomes or two covers, which cannot share a column, still mean either.

## New in 1.2.0

**The Terrain Generator: a new terrain generator, with composite nodes you can open (experimental)**

The Terrain side opens a new generator, the Terrain Generator (marked experimental; the graph editor you know stays in the area picker as Classic graph, and its graphs open in the new one migrated). Its graph ends in one Map Output with an input for each thing the map takes: height, water, the colour of the ground, terrains, biomes, climate, layers of rock, ground covers and objects, caves and cave biomes, volumes to carve or add, structures and roads, and masks. Its nodes are the shapes mountain maps are made of (ranges along a drawn crest, peaks, volcanoes, mesas, canyons, glacial valleys, dunes, karst, craters, islands, coasts), adjustments, simulations (stream and thermal erosion, water flow), climate, masks, colours, points scattered over the terrain and volumes. Composite nodes hold a graph of their own that a double click opens: Massif ships Alpine Range, Cave System and Village Generator, and any nodes can be gathered into a composite of your own, with the settings you choose to show. Previews are lit like a render and come back while you edit; Apply writes the result into the map window by window, so that maps of tens of thousands of blocks fit in memory, as one step to undo.

**The terrain graph editor, rebuilt for composites**

The new terrain generator's graph editor works with composites, as Gaea's and World Machine's do. Select nodes and press ⌘G to make a composite of them, one node that holds them; double-click it to open it, with a breadcrumb back out, its inputs and outputs as columns at the edges, and expose any setting inside so that every node of it shows it as its own. Massif's Mountain opens read only, and Edit a copy makes it the world's own. Frames take a title, a colour and a note, sit in other frames, fold to their title and move with what they hold. Nodes take a name of their own, can be bypassed (B), snap to the grid, line up and arrange themselves in columns, and copy and paste as JSON, between worlds too. Each kind of socket has its colour and shape, points, lines, footprints, instances and volumes included, and a wire an input cannot take says why and which node to put between them. Apply to map writes everything the Map Output carries in one step you can undo: the ground window by window, so that large maps never have to fit in memory whole, then caves, cave biomes and carved or added volumes, then the villages and their roads, replacing those an earlier Apply laid and keeping those placed by hand; a dialog shows how far it is and Cancel leaves the map as it was. Thumbnails show points, lines, footprints and buildings over the relief, and a volume as its cut. The 3D views gain Objects, which shows or hides the trees, bushes and rocks of the layers, and Density, which colours the land by how many objects its layers will place, with a scale, so that you see how thick each forest will be before exporting. The Terrain side now opens on the Generator workspace, the new Terrain Generator, marked Experimental, and the samples and templates of the home screen open there with their graph and its preview instead of jumping to the World side; the generator of earlier versions stays in the area picker as Classic graph, for older maps.

**The Terrain Generator in panels of its own**

The Terrain Generator is now four panels like the rest of Massif: the Node Library, the Generator Viewer, the Generator Graph (with its MassifScript pane) and Node Properties. Each can be moved, swapped, put in tabs, floated or closed, and they keep working together wherever they are: selecting a node shows its settings and its terrain, Live and Apply work from the viewer, and undo over any of them undoes the graph's last change. The Generator workspace lays them out as before, and a layout saved with the generator in one area opens split into the four. The classic graph's settings panel is now named Classic properties.

**MassifScript: the terrain graph as text, and a guide for any AI**

The Terrain Generator's graph can now be read and written as a script, in a small C-like language of its own: `base = FractalNoise(scale: 2400, height: 600);` makes a node, `eroded = StreamErosion(base);` feeds another, `group "Geology" { … }` frames them, `output height = eroded;` sends the relief to the map, and components, constants, conditions, loops and imports build more at once. The script button beside the graph shows it as a script that follows the graph; what you type is checked as you type, mistakes underlined with their line and column and the name you probably meant, and Apply makes the graph from it in one step you can undo, the nodes you had keeping their places. A script makes exactly the nodes, links, frames and composites the editor makes, and every graph can be written back as a script. Copy for AI copies a guide to paste into any AI chat (every node with its settings, examples and your graph), so that it can answer with a script to paste and apply. `.mscript` files open and save from the pane, and `massif-cli mscript guide`, `build`, `check` and `decompile` do the same from the command line.

**Zooming and moving around the terrain graph**

In the Terrain Generator, a mouse wheel or a pinch now zooms the graph around the pointer, from far enough out to see a large graph whole to close enough to read every node's settings; two fingers on a trackpad move it, ⌘+ and ⌘− zoom, ⌘0 goes back to full size, and F, the frame button or a double-click on the empty ground shows the whole graph. The minimap sits at the bottom left, outlines the part in view, moves the view where you click or drag, no longer jumps from side to side, and lets the wheel zoom the graph over it. The viewer's 3D camera keeps its distance as it turns instead of coming closer and going away, its background is plain dark by default (the sky is a choice in its menu), and its resolution can be raised to 2048, 4096 or 8192 samples a side, as the classic graph's preview can, with a word on the memory and time they take. In a node's settings the sliders all start at the same place and stay put as you drag them. While you draw a wire near the Map Output, its folded groups that can take it open by themselves and the inputs that take it glow, so that you find where caves or structures plug in; folded groups say how many inputs they hold. A graph without a Map Output says so, with a button that adds one. Delete removes a selected frame too, and ⌘X cuts nodes in one step you can undo.

**Caves as the game carves them, painted, with lakes, cave biomes and their decoration**

Caves are now a layer you paint: the Caves tool (in the new Underground group) paints where a cave layer carves its caves, and Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Caves paints one over the whole map or the selection, after a picture of its caves (a plan at a height you pick and a cut through the land). A layer carves caves as Minecraft does since 1.18 — large chambers with pillars, long winding tunnels, thin noodles and ravines, each with its density, size and heights — under a roof of rock except where they open to the sky on dry land, and fills them with aquifers: water, and lava deep down, at levels of their own, walled off from each other by rock so that nothing runs once the game updates a block. Its settings change the caves wherever it is painted, at any time, and the caves take no room in the file. The Cave biome tool paints lush caves, dripstone caves and the deep dark between two heights; the export writes the game's cave biomes and decorates their caves as the game does: moss, azaleas, glow berries and dripleaves by clay pools; dripstone blocks with stalactites and stalagmites thick at their base; sculk, veins, sensors, shriekers and catalysts with their block entities; glow lichen in other caves. Underground on the 2D map cuts it through at a height, and X-ray in the 3D views shows the caves through the ground. The Ores window adds the game's large veins of copper in granite and iron in tuff. WorldPainter's Caverns, Chasms and Caves layers open as cave layers painted where they were.

**Caves in the terrain graph.** The new terrain generator makes caves: a Cave layer node holds the settings of a cave layer (chambers, tunnels, noodles, ravines, roof, surface entrances, sealed aquifers and a lava floor) and a mask of where its caves go, a Cave biome node paints lush caves, dripstone caves or the deep dark between two heights, and the Cave System composite puts the game's caves under a relief with lush caves under wet ground and the deep dark under the mountains, its densities, depths, water and lava as settings. Volume nodes carve what cave layers cannot: a tunnel along a drawn line, a great hall, cave noise kept to a band of rock, rock added for arches. Apply writes them into the map, keeping the caves painted by hand, and they export as painted caves do.

**Edit the map layer by layer.** The new Layer tool (Underground group) shows the 2D map cut at a height — PageUp and PageDown move it a layer, Shift eight — with rock, caves, water, lava and the blocks' colours, and its brush digs, fills with a block, pours water or lava or paints a cave biome on that layer or on the layers around it, as a ball with a round brush. Each stroke is one step to undo. Caves made by the terrain graph show there too, and what you fix by hand stays when the graph is applied again.

**One Structures tool for villages and the game's structures, no selection needed**

The village brush and the Structure tool are one tool now, **Structures**, in the Decor group. Pick a village theme (the game's, or a builder's pack) or one of the game's structures in its list, then click on the map to place it — a village of the size chosen (Small, Medium, Large), centred on the click — or drag a rectangle for a village over it; a selection can still be filled with **Fill the selection**. Click a village or a structure placed to select it: drag it to move it, drag a village's corners to resize it, change its houses, roads (dirt, gravel, stone), walls or draw, and it is built again; **Take it away** removes it and gives the land back as it was. Underground ones (a stronghold, an Ancient City, Trial Chambers) go at the height set. Village packs say more too: buildings sorted by size, farms with fields, market stalls, mills, lampposts and carts, road styles, and a check that lists what is wrong in a pack, file by file. `massif-cli village-pack-from-game` and `village-pack-from-world` make packs from the game's own villages or from a world where a builder laid out their builds, to try villages with. The village's settings say what it will build: a line such as "Medium village · 18 houses · 1 church · 2 farms · stone roads · walls", how many of each type of building (a pack's counts can be set: farms, forges, market stalls…), the pack's buildings with their sizes, how much flat, dry land it needs, and whether the land under a placed village holds the houses asked for.

**Structures and the village brush: the game's villages, Ancient Cities, Trial Chambers and more, one click each**

The new Structure tool (Decor group) places the game's own structures where you click, on the map or in the 3D view: the five villages, a pillager outpost, the desert and jungle temples, a witch hut, an igloo, shipwrecks, ocean ruins, an Ancient City with its warden, Trial Chambers, a stronghold with its End portal, trail ruins and bastion remnants. Massif reads them from your own Minecraft (and your mods') and assembles them the way the game does, piece by piece: their chests keep their loot tables, spawners their mobs, villages their villagers, and the Ancient City's sculk shriekers summon the warden. Its outline follows the pointer before you click, villages and temples sit on levelled ground, an Ancient City is carved into the deep dark at y −52, and each placement is one step to undo; a right-click takes one away. The village brush, beside it, fills a selection with a village sized by it — a hamlet, a village, or a town of several districts — with roads that follow the land, buildings facing them, villagers and, if you want them, walls with towers and gates; its themes are the game's villages or a builder's pack of schematics (the format is in the guide's Village packs page). `massif-cli structure` and `massif-cli village` do the same from the command line, and `tools/minecraft_check.py --structures` has the game itself confirm them.

**Villages: their size sets how close the houses stand, and a new theme rebuilds them at once**

A village's Size is now how close its houses stand: a small village has a few houses far apart, a large one many houses close together, and the number of houses follows its land. Dragging a village's corners keeps that density, adding houses over more land and taking some away over less; a number typed in Houses stays as typed until you let it follow the land again. Clicking another theme or pack in the list while a village is selected builds it again of that theme, in its place, without drawing it again. In the Tools panel, the names of the rows sit in a column as wide as the longest in your language, so every row's tools start at the same place.

**Villages: a fence, a hedge or a low wall round them rather than ramparts**

A village's Walls are now picked from a menu, each with a small picture: a wooden fence, a spruce fence, post and rail, a hedge, a flowering hedge, a low stone wall, a dry-stone wall, stone and fence, a palisade, or the ramparts with towers of before. Each is made of the game's own blocks with a little variety along its run (posts, lanterns, mossy stones, logs of different heights), and has a gate wherever a road crosses it: a fence gate across the road, an arch of leaves through a hedge, a beam over a palisade's. Villages placed before keep their ramparts. The terrain graph's Village walls node and the command line (`--enclosure`) offer the same styles.

**The Building tool: move, turn, swap or remove one building of a village**

A new Building tool, beside Structures, changes one building of a village placed from a pack. Click a building to select it, then drag it to move it (a path is laid from its door to the nearest road), press R to turn it about its middle, or Delete to take it away. Tool Settings puts another building of the pack in its place from a menu showing each one from above with its size, draws another building of its type, or puts it back as the village's draw placed it. Each change is one step to undo, and the village keeps it when it is built again: moved, resized, of another theme or with other walls, the same buildings are changed the same way.

**WorldPainter maps keep every layer of every block**

A WorldPainter world comes in with every layer of every block, each with its own intensity: a block painted with a forest at 50 %, bushes at 15 % and 8 % and three ground covers keeps all of them, rather than the one Massif kept before. Covers lie over each other as WorldPainter lays them (Conquest Reforged's grass layers on the ground, plants on them, frost on top) and the export places each one, and the Info panel lists them all. Ground covers of layer blocks (Conquest Reforged's `*_layer` blocks, snow layers, mixes of several) are now found even when Conquest Reforged is not read in the Blocks panel, and are offered first in the import report to become the ground's own; Edit ▸ Covers of Layers to Ground… offers them at any time. The import report is kept with the map and File ▸ Import Report… shows it again. Custom biomes come in as biomes of the map, exported by their ids, and any biome of the map that is not the game's can be renamed and recoloured (map, grass, leaves) with a right-click in the Biomes panel. WorldPainter objects of its own kind and custom annotation layers, which were dropped, come in too. A map of many imported objects no longer spends several milliseconds every frame checking whether its layers changed. Every custom layer keeps the colour WorldPainter shows it in, and a ground cover its opacity, rather than Massif's greens.

**Your mods' ground blocks in the Terrain panel, and WorldPainter worlds sorted by mod**

The Terrain panel now lists, under the map's terrains, the blocks of your game and mods that make ground, by mod and category: stone, soil, wood and building blocks, without the glass, lamps, furniture, doors, slabs and plants that only cluttered the list. Click one to paint with it; it becomes a terrain of the map in its category. Every block shows the rest, and the search finds any block. A WorldPainter world made of a mod's blocks now says so on import and offers to read the mod first, and its long Imported list is sorted by mod and kind in one click. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).

**Sort the Terrain panel your way**

The Terrain panel's categories are now yours, saved with the map: drag a terrain onto another category, or right-click it and choose Move to, to sort it there or into a new category; rename a category (double-click its title), move it up or down, fold it, hide its terrains or delete it, its terrains going to Other. Hide from the list takes a terrain you never use out of the lists without touching the map; it waits under Hidden at the end of the panel. A WorldPainter world's long Imported list can at last be sorted. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).

**Replace one terrain with another over the whole map**

Edit ▸ Replace terrain… paints every column of one terrain with another, over the whole map, or only in the selection when there is one, in one step to undo. Pick both terrains from lists sorted by category, with a search. It is the way to merge duplicates, such as a terrain a WorldPainter world brought as Imported and the same block read from a mod. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).

**Game & mods has a window of its own; Terrain and Blocks say what they are for**

The version of Minecraft, the mods, the modpack instances and the resource packs whose blocks you paint with are now set up in File ▸ Game & mods…, also opened by a button at the top of the Blocks panel, which keeps only the blocks to paint with and says which game and how many mods it read. The Terrain panel and the Blocks panel each open with a line saying what they are for: Terrain is the map's terrains, Blocks every block of your game and its mods, to paint with. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).

**Smooth terrain knows Conquest Reforged's block families**

Smooth terrain and Make them the ground's own now read which block each layer, slab and stair is cut from in the mods' own stonecutter recipes, so they find the shapes a mod names otherwise: with Conquest Reforged, the game's stone is smoothed by eighths with its limestone slab, terracottas with their hardened clay slabs, and blocks that only have a slab by eighths (brown moss, dark mud) use it as layers, where many areas stayed whole before. Covers of layers turned into ground rise as WorldPainter lays them, from the land's precise height by eighths, rather than a whole block over it (the forest floors stood a block above the land around), and covers of Conquest's `_slab` blocks can be turned into ground too. Painting a ground cover's plants on smoothed land no longer takes its layers away: the plants stand on them, in the 3D view and in the export.

**Plants sit on layers, and annotation layers have names**

Conquest Reforged's plants now sit on the layers under them wherever they grow: on the layers Smooth terrain lays, on a cover of layer blocks, or on a terrain whose top is a block of layers, each plant is written with the eighths of the block under it, with nothing to set up (no plant layers exported first or materials file as in WorldPainter). The game's plants, which cannot sit lower, keep a whole block under them rather than floating. Annotations can be layers of their own, as WorldPainter's custom annotation layers: + beside Annotations in the Layers panel makes one with its name and colour, listed there to paint with, rename, recolour and show or hide on its own; a WorldPainter world brings its custom annotation layers in as such, by name.

**Block states for ground covers, as WorldPainter's block picker**

A ground cover's blocks are edited with their states: click a row of Grows (or add a block) and each property of its block shows under the list — layers, facing, half, waterlogged, age… — with the values it allows, read from the game's and the mods' files (KubeJS blocks and WorldPainter block lists too). Default leaves a property to the game, the resulting id with its properties is written under them, and each row shows its properties after its name instead of hiding them in a tooltip. Random, beside facing, rotation, age and the like, grows the block every way: one row for each value, sharing the weight.

**A wide window for object layers of hundreds of schematics**

An object layer's Settings… now opens a wide window: on the left, the layer's objects in a tall list as high as the window, with a search and a sort (as imported, by name, by height, by frequency), each row with its picture, its measures, its tree size and its share; on the right, the layer's settings and, under them, those of the objects picked, with the same picking as before (click, Shift+Click, Shift+Arrows, ⌘/Ctrl+Click). Drag its corner to make it bigger: it opens again at that size. Tree sizes of your own are made where they are used: New size… at the end of an object's Tree size list adds one and gives it to the objects picked, and New size under Density of each size adds one to the map.

**Solo a layer, as in WorldPainter**

Alt-click a layer's eye in the Layers panel, or choose Solo in its menu, and that layer is the only cover or tree and object layer drawn on the 2D map and in the 3D views, the terrain still drawn; a combined layer shows the cover and trees it paints. The map's header shows Solo: and the layer's name. Alt-click the eye again, choose Show all layers, or click the chip in the map's header, and every layer comes back shown or hidden exactly as it was before. A palette's solo (Alt-click its eye) works the same way now, and a WorldPainter world whose palette was soloed opens soloed, ready to come back. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).

**Import a Minecraft world**

File ▸ Import Minecraft World… (and Import a Minecraft world… on the home screen) makes a map of a Minecraft Java world, as WorldPainter's Import ▸ Existing Minecraft map: pick its folder, or drop it, its level.dat or a region file on the window. A dialog asks for the dimension, the area (the whole world, or drawn on a map of its chunks), the heights, and what becomes of what stands above the ground: kept block for block as sculpted chunks, so buildings, trees and overhangs come back unchanged on export; trees made object layers of the world's own trees, by kind; or dropped. Each column gets its ground's height, its top block as a terrain (the map's own where one has that block on top, a new one otherwise, mods' blocks kept), its water or lava and its biome (custom biomes kept); plants, snow and carpets become ground covers, mixed grounds can become terrains that mix them, and caves can be kept too. Worlds of 1.12 and older to 26.x are read, large ones region by region with progress and cancel, and the import report lists what came in, the terrains made and the blocks left out.

**The views load around what they show**

On a huge map the 3D views, the Diorama and the Render no longer try to build the whole map before they rest. A 3D view builds the land within the view distance of its camera, the nearest first, and shows the rest at most as the quick first look the 2D map gives; the Diorama builds the tiles in view and a margin around them; the Render holds and builds only the part of the map within the view distance of the point its camera looks at, and makes it again around the new place once the camera has gone far. Once what they show is ready they stop, and the processor rests. Move, and they build the new place. The Diorama and the Render also open without their second-long pause on such a map. The 2D map draws close up a map with many object layers, as WorldPainter imports them, up to 150 times faster: each image of the map went through every spot of every object layer, painted there or not, and took up to a quarter of a second on Middle-earth; it now looks only where each layer is painted, and draws the very same trees. **Settings ▸ Graphics ▸ Load** chooses between **Around the view** (the default, with a view distance of 1,024 to 8,192 blocks) and **The whole map**, as before, for flying over all of it at length. Asked for by Jack on his Middle-earth of 53,888 × 43,008 blocks.

**Test Export starts at once on a huge map**

A Test Export of a few region files no longer sits at 0 % on a large map: before writing its first tile it worked out the water of the whole map, which took minutes on a map of Middle-earth's size and longer still with sculpted ground. It now works out the water of the tiles it writes and of those around them that their water depends on, and writes them exactly as a full export does: one region of a 16,384-block map is done in about a second instead of more than a minute. The progress counts that water too, so a full export's bar moves from the start, and Cancel stops it at any point.

**Great lakes from a real place are water all over.** Relief of a real place left most of a large lake dry, with water only in odd rectangles and pieces cut along straight lines: around the Straits of Mackinac, with the real height at the sea level set to the lakes' 176 m, Lakes Michigan and Huron came out as green land. The elevation data gives such a lake's surface in rectangles of its sources, each flat at a level of its own a little apart, and each was taken for a terrace rather than a lake. Those rectangles now make one lake, at one level, its floor dug under it and its water reaching its shore, in a new world as over an existing map; and a wide flat at the real height you put at the sea level is water, even where it meets the lake's charted depths or the edge of the area. Many more small inland lakes come out as water too, and a lake's water no longer stands a block over its shore.

**The window of a new version is sized to yours**

Clicking the notice of a new version, on the home screen or at the top right of the editor, opens its notes in a window sized to Massif's: wide, the notes filling its height and scrolling, with Open the release page, Later and Skip this version under them. Before, the notes sat in a small slot in the middle of the screen, the home screen's preview showing beside it. A build as new as the latest release, or newer, is never told of an older one.

## New in 1.1.1

**Show or hide a whole palette at once**

Each palette in the Layers panel has an eye on its title, as in WorldPainter: a click hides or shows every layer in it at once, ground covers and tree and object layers alike, on the 2D map and in the 3D views, just as each layer's own eye does. When some of its layers are hidden and others shown, the eye is drawn half, and a click shows them all. Alt-click the eye, or choose Show only this palette in its menu, to show that palette alone, as WorldPainter's solo; do it again and every layer comes back. A WorldPainter world keeps its palettes hidden or soloed as they were. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).


**The Eyedropper tool works as WorldPainter's**

The Eyedropper tool (⌥Y) now picks what you want to paint with. Click the 2D map or a 3D view and a small list by the pointer shows what is there: its terrain, its biome, and every layer painted there (ground cover, trees, under the trees, tree size, pockets, annotation, combined layer). Click one and its tool is chosen with it, ready to paint: Paint terrain, Paint biome or the layer's own tool. Where there is only a terrain, it is picked at once. Shift-click does what the Eyedropper did before: it takes the terrain, height and water at once and goes back to your tool. Alt-click while painting works as before. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).


**Smoother on maps of many imported objects**

A map holding many objects imported from WorldPainter (schematics with their own rules) no longer spends several milliseconds of every frame checking whether its layers changed: on Jack's ArdaCraft recording that was 5.8 ms a frame, a third of a frame's time at 60 fps, even with nothing moving.


**Paint terrain: pick the terrain in place, and paint by zones**

The terrain Paint terrain lays, at the top of its Tool Settings, is now a button: a click opens a list to search every terrain and block, the ones picked lately first, without going to the Blocks panel (the map's terrain under Right button picks the same way). A new way to paint, **Zones**, lays each column with the terrain its height, its slope and the water over it call for, from presets — Classic, Plains, Mountain (grass, gravel and stone on slopes, snow on the peaks), Mesa (red sand and bands of terracotta), Desert, Taiga, Coast — or from zones of your own, listed and edited in Tool Settings, kept with the map and saved under a name for other maps. The right button's By height paints the same zones. Grass, snow and the like are never painted under water any more, a lake above the sea included: sand, clay, dirt and gravel by depth, as in the game.


**The game is found beside your modpack's instance, whatever the launcher**

On a PC whose launcher keeps Minecraft somewhere Massif did not look, the Blocks panel listed the modpack's instances but said "No Minecraft installation was found", and Use read nothing. Massif now looks for the game beside each instance it finds and wherever the launchers keep it: the official launcher, CurseForge on any drive or folder, the Modrinth App (which keeps the game under the loader's name, such as 1.20.1-fabric-0.16.10), Prism, MultiMC, ATLauncher and GDLauncher. Use reads the instance over the version of the game it plays; when that version is not on the computer, the panel says which one to start once in the launcher or to choose with Choose…. Reported by Jack (Fornad).

## New in 1.1.0

**Work on one map together (beta)**

Several people can now work on the same map and join their work. The owner keeps the map; contributors start from one of its versions and send their changes back as a small `.massifpatch` file (Versions ▸ Export my changes…), only the tiles they changed: about 2 MB for 1,000 × 1,000 blocks reshaped on a real map. The owner brings it in (Import a contribution…) and reviews it on the map: the changed areas drawn over the 2D map, new, changed or in conflict where both changed the same land, each accepted or rejected, a conflict settled with mine, theirs or tile by tile, the settings of the map it changes switched on one by one. Applying it is one step to undo and a new version. A zone sent to World Machine or Gaea comes back the same way: Export Region keeps a version and writes zone.json beside the images, and the images brought back are compared with that version and reviewed before anything changes. A shared folder (Google Drive, Dropbox, iCloud, Git) can hold the published map and the contributions, so that nobody sends files by hand. Save points are now the map's versions: each shows who made it, the one the map stands on and the merges. A part of a big map can go to someone as a map of its own: File ▸ Export Region… as a Massif map writes the selection and a border of tiles around it, at its place, with the map's terrains, layers and versions; File ▸ Merge Massif Map… brings their work back, with the map shown before and after, the changed tiles outlined, conflicts marked, each area accepted or rejected, and the terrains and layers they made added to the map.

**Tools for WorldPainter terraformers**

The Info panel is now WorldPainter's inspector: it follows the cursor over the 2D map and the 3D view and shows the column's coordinates, height, water, terrain, biome (painted or automatic), whether it is selected, and every layer painted there — cover, trees, under the trees, tree size, pockets, smoothed steps, combined layers, annotation — with its intensity; the world's name, seed, sea level, spawn, blocks, size and memory moved to File ▸ World Information…. A stroke all outside the selection now says why nothing happens. Brush filters can be on layers too (ferns, tall grass, tree and object layers, pockets, annotations), their list is searchable and sorted with what the map holds first, by recent use or A–Z, and an eyedropper picks what the filter is on by clicking the map or the 3D view. Right-click a layer ▸ Find takes the map to the nearest place it is painted, then the next. The new Pencil (Brush Settings) draws an unbroken hard line that follows the mouse, one block wide and joined by the blocks' sides, with any tool. Alt and the wheel turn the brush, as in WorldPainter, and Ctrl and the wheel zoom. The map's grid shows the region files' borders (512 blocks) with their names, r.x.z.mca, for merging maps, and Test Export can pick whole regions on the map, or round any part out to them, listing the region files it writes.

**Palettes, every object setting of WorldPainter, and tree sizes of your own**

Layers sort into **palettes**, as in WorldPainter: named groups at the top of the Layers panel that fold, rename and move, holding layers of any kind; drag a layer onto one, or use Palette in its menu, and a palette deleted sends its layers back to their sections. Your brush groups work the same way: fold them, rename or delete them, drag a brush to another. A WorldPainter world or layer file keeps its palettes. An object layer now lists its objects in a compact list: click one to edit it, Shift+Click, Shift+Arrows or Cmd/Ctrl+Click to edit several at once, with each object's frequency, origin and, with Own rules, every attribute of WorldPainter's object dialog — turned and mirrored at random or fixed, raised and varied in height or at a fixed height, on land, on air, under or on water and lava, what it collides with and replaces underground, its leaves, waterlogging, joined fences and a block placed as air; WorldPainter's objects come in with all of them. **Tree sizes** are yours to define: add sizes such as Tiny, Forest or Open-grown, set each object's size by hand (Auto still guesses from its height), and give each size its own density in a layer's settings. Trees can now be spaced **by canopy**: Massif measures each tree's crown from its leaves (or takes the radius you set), and two neighbours stand as far apart as their crowns need, so that crowns touch without overlapping and narrow trees no longer stand as far apart as broad ones; a least gap keeps trunks apart. Layers of objects you import are spaced by canopy; older layers keep their grid until you switch them.

**True Colour view**

The 2D map and the 3D views have a new mode, True Colour, that shows the map as it will look in the game once exported rather than in Massif's editor colours: every block in its texture's colour, and grass, leaves, vines and water tinted by the biome they stand in, as the game does (a River biome no longer makes grass blue). Resource packs added in the Blocks panel change these colours in their order, the last one winning as in the game, including OptiFine's custom colour maps for grass, leaves and any block they name; mods' blocks show in their own textures' colours. The Render side tints its blocks with the same colour maps. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).

**KubeJS blocks and connected textures from modpacks.** Reading an instance (**Use** in the Blocks panel, or **Instance…**) now also reads the blocks its KubeJS scripts make, listed as a mod named KubeJS: the blocks its startup scripts register, with the names, shapes and textures the scripts give them, and the states, models and textures written in its `kubejs/assets` folder; a resource pack left as a folder, given to **Add mods…**, reads too. Connected textures made for Fusion or OptiFine (CTM, read by Continuity too) show as in the game: each block shows one tile at its real size in the Blocks panel (Fusion's sheets were drawn whole on each block, shrunk eight times), and in the True Colour view each top shows the tiles its neighbours give it. Thanks to nicolas-vinc, who wrote the reading of KubeJS's folder and of Fusion's sheets.

**Annotations in any colour, with their opacity, drawn as curves; sharper contour lines**

Annotations now show in the 3D views too, and an eye in the Annotations tool's settings (also the pen button in the map's header, and View ▸ Show Annotations) shows or hides them all at once; each colour has its own opacity in the tool's settings. Besides WorldPainter's fifteen colours, the Colour button picks any colour, which the map keeps with its own. The Annotations tool can also draw curves, as Axiom's Path tool: click points on the map, move them, add or take some off, and pick a smooth curve through every point, Bézier handles or straight lines, with a width at its start and another at its end; it shows as the ribbon it will paint until you press Enter, then becomes an annotation like any other. The contour lines are now WorldPainter's: a solid dark line every 10 blocks and a finer one halfway, readable at every zoom; the arrow beside their button sets the interval (5, 10, 20, 50 or any), their strength, black or white lines, crisp or smooth edges.

**World rules in the export: no more /gamerule after each export**

The export dialog has a Rules tab: the game mode, the difficulty, and the world's game rules, written into the world so that it opens as set. Pick a preset, Creative / Frozen (nothing spawns, spreads, grows or decays, no weather nor day going by, noon for good: to walk round a map as it was built), Survival safe (fire does not spread, mobs break no blocks) or Vanilla, or set each rule: mobs, pillager patrols, the wandering trader, phantoms, mobs changing blocks, fire spreading, random ticks, keeping one's inventory, the day and the weather going by, the time of day and the weather. Save a set of rules under your own name with Save as preset… (Settings ▸ Export lists them), and each map keeps the rules of its last export. They are written as each version of Minecraft names them, the new names of 1.21.11 and the file of their own of 26.1 included.

**Smoother brushes, and a performance recorder**

Painting and sculpting with a large brush no longer drags the whole window down when the Diorama or the Render side is open: those views now rebuild what a stroke changed a few times a second and on their own threads, instead of compressing the edited tiles and taking the brush's own processor time every frame, and raising land no longer looks for water to fill at each touch of the brush. On a 4,096-block map with a 100-block brush, a stroke took a third of the processor time it took before. When Massif still stutters, **Help ▸ Record Performance…** records it: start it, do what is slow, click the red dot at the top right to stop, and a `.zip` lands on your desktop with every frame and where its time went, your computer and settings, the map's size and what you did, never the map itself, to send us in #bug-reports.

**WorldPainter's overlay images come with the world.** Importing a `.world` brings the surface's overlay images (WorldPainter's View ▸ Overlays) as reference images of the map, at the same place, scale and opacity, shown or hidden as they were. Their files are looked for where WorldPainter had them, then by name beside the `.world`, so a world made on Windows finds its pictures on a Mac when they travel with it. One that is not found keeps its place and is named in the import report; **Find its file…**, in the reference image's settings, links it again.

**Layers laid over the land as WorldPainter ground covers can become the land itself.** A WorldPainter map made for Conquest Reforged often lays a block's layers over the land as a custom ground cover (`grass_block_layer` over grass, snow layers): imported, the land stood a block lower than it looked, and Massif's tools did not know its height. The import report now lists those covers, ticked; **Make them the ground's own** raises each column by its layers' eighths, puts the full block on top (keeping the terrain when it already is that block) and smooths it with layers on export, so the exported world looks as before while the map, the 3D view, the brushes and Smooth terrain follow the land's true height. Untick a cover to keep it a cover; it is one step to undo.

**Linked map sizes, snowfall, noise gradients**

The width and depth of a new map, of a new world from a real place and of a map resized are linked by a chain: typing one sets the other, until you click the chain to set them apart. Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Snowfall… lays snow as the wind and the slopes leave it — drifts in the lee of ridges and in hollows, bare windward slopes, none on steep cliffs or over water —, in snow layers then snow blocks, within a band of heights, with a preview first and one step to undo. Noise painting has a Blend that turns its list into an ordered gradient (dirt, then coarse dirt, then grass, dithered between neighbours), and the same mix is the terrain graph's new Noise paint node, which shares its presets with the brush.

**Every typeface fits the smallest window.** In Inter, Geist, IBM Plex Sans or Manrope (Settings ▸ Typeface), a few things took more room than the narrowest sidebar or the smallest window gave them: the selection tools' Invert folded onto two lines in Russian, the links under a new map ran past the window's edge in French, and Export Region grew taller than a window of 640 points, its buttons scrolling out of view with the rest. The selection tools' buttons now go to the next line whole, the links take a second line when they need one, and Export Region's settings scroll under buttons that stay in view.

## New in 1.0.0

**The Gradient brush is easy to find.** It sat in the Paint row behind an icon of two circles that said little. It now has an icon of its own, a swatch fading from full to empty, marked with a dot until you first try it, and its card says it is new. Paint terrain's Tool Settings also offer it as a third way to paint, beside **One terrain** and **Noise**, and the Gradient brush shows the same choice to go back. The tour and the help point to it.

**Unpainting gives back the map's own terrain.** The right button of Paint terrain used to put back the terrain the height calls for, so on a map filled with rock, unpainting a high place turned it to snow. It now puts back the map's own terrain: the one a new map was filled with, or, on a map made before, the one covering nearly all of it. Tool Settings shows which under **Right button**, where **Change** picks another and **By height** brings back the old way, which maps made from their height keep. 3D Sculpt's Paint does the same.
